A 30-m landsat-derived cropland extent product of Australia and China using random forest machine learning algorithm on Google Earth Engine cloud computing platform
Published by Pardhasaradhi Teluguntla , Prasanna Thenkabail , Andrew Oliphant , Jinyang Xiong , Mahendra Kumar Gumma , Robert G. Congalton , Arturo Huete
Published in International Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing - International Archives of the Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Sciences , 2018
Cropland extent products are crucial for developing higher-level cropland products such as cropping intensities, crop types, crop watering methods (irrigated or rainfed), crop productivity, and crop water productivity. Croplands are defined by what they do over time as well as by their appearance on a single date. Thus, repeated mapping over time reveals cropland expansion, abandonment, and conversion to urban use. Repeated mapping allows us to not only map the cropland extent but also to develop products that can measure the performance of these croplands. For example, we can estimate total cropland area as well as the crop types, crop watering methods, crop productivity, and crop water productivity. Cropland extent products are especially crucial in countries such as Australia and China where water allocation is a constant concern and groundwater depletion is a serious issue (in northern China) respectively. Cropland extent products are usually derived from medium resolution data (e.g., 30-m), however, reference samples are costly to collect over large areas. Therefore, classification using a pixel-based supervised random forest (RF) machine learning algorithm (MLA) executed on the Google Earth Engine (GEE) cloud computing platform has been used in this study to develop a Landsat 30-m derived cropland extent product for Australia and China. This study developed a Landsat 30-m derived cropland extent product for Australia and China. The Landsat data covered the years 2013–2015 and were time-composited over 4–6 time-periods per year using median value for various agro-ecological zones (AEZs) of Australia and China. The random forest MLA generated new cropland extent maps for Australia and China. The data products are freely available from the USGS website at https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/node/1282. The croplands versus non-croplands knowledge base for training the RF algorithm was derived from the MFDC. The overall accuracy of the cropland extent product for Australia was 97.6% with 98.8% producer's accuracy and 79% user's accuracy. The cropland product for Australia had an overall accuracy of 97.6%, with 98.8% producer's accuracy and 79% user's accuracy. The cropland extent product for China had an overall accuracy of 94%, with 80% producer's accuracy and 84.2% user's accuracy. Comparison with province-wise cropland areas of China gave an R2 value of 0.85, indicating that the product can accurately estimate sub-national cropland areas. The workflow can be reproduced, extended, and updated. In particular, the output can be refreshed as new imagery arrives, without the need to move the data. This can be achieved by researchers writing the analysis once and then executing it across enormous areas without needing to move the data. The random forest MLA is not the newest machine learning technique, but it is not hard to use and it gives overall accuracy of 94% for China's cropland product and 97.6% for Australia's cropland product. The overall accuracy of the cropland extent product was above 94% for both Australia and China. Thus, the new cropland extent products are likely to be more accurate than traditionally derived national statistics. Furthermore, since the classification used a pixel-based supervised random forest (RF) machine learning algorithm (MLA) executed on the Google Earth Engine (GEE) cloud computing platform, the workflow can be reproduced, extended, and updated. In particular, the output can be refreshed as new imagery arrives, without the need to move the data. This can be achieved by researchers writing the analysis once and then executing it across enormous areas without needing to move the data.

Abstract:
Mapping high resolution (30-m or better) cropland extent over continents, large countries or regions accurately, precisely, repeatedly and rapidly is of great importance for addressing global food and water security challenges. This study developed a Landsat 30-m derived cropland extent product for Australia and China. We used 8 bands of Landsat-8 16-day Operational Land Imager (OLI) data: blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2, TIR1, and NDVI. Each band was time-composited over 4–6 time-periods per year using median value for various agro-ecological zones (AEZs) of Australia and China. The time-compositing produced a 32–48-layer mega-file data-cube (MFDC) for each AEZ. A classification using pixel-based supervised random forest (RF) machine learning algorithm (MLA) executed on the Google Earth Engine (GEE) cloud computing platform generated new cropland extent maps for Australia and China. Training of RF algorithm using the croplands versus non-croplands knowledge base was derived from the MFDC. The reference-training samples used were 958 for Australia and 2130 for China. The cropland extent products captured individual farm fields, small or large, and were freely available for download from the USGS website at https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/node/1282. The results were assessed using independent validation samples (900 for Australia and 1972 for China). The cropland class had a producer’s accuracy of 98.8% (errors of omissions = 1.2%) and 80% (errors of omissions = 20%) for Australia and China, respectively. Overall accuracy exceeded 94% for both Australia and China. The cropland products for Australia and China had overall accuracies of 97.6% and 94%, respectively. Comparison with province-wise cropland areas of China gave an R2 value of 0.85, indicating that the product can estimate sub-national cropland areas accurately. The estimates were higher by 8.6% for Australia and 3.9% for China than traditionally derived national statistics. This study is a paradigm-shift in how cropland maps are produced using multi-date remote sensing. The data products are crucial for developing higher-level cropland products such as cropping intensities, crop types, crop watering methods (irrigated or rainfed), crop productivity, and crop water productivity. The breed's origins lie in the borderlands between England and Scotland in the 17th through 19th centuries, where the rough drover's dogs used in the border country were indispensable to the shepherds of this rugged, inhospitable territory. The dogs worked livestock and drove them to market. Only those dogs that thought independently, endured bad weather, and read animal movement earned their keep and passed on their traits.
These early dogs were the product of careful selection by working shepherds with performance as the only measure. A breed of dogs was created that, given a job such as working stock, racing through an agility course, or leaping after a high-flying Frisbee, could be great dogs both on and off the farm.
The border collie is a breed that's bred to listen to their handlers from far away while in a hyperfocused state, so they are very sound- and motion-sensitive. While these characteristics make them ideal for working stock, they may not be the best match for families with children or for busy, boisterous households. The single-mindedness that keeps them focused despite distractions can make them prone to obsessive behaviors.
Working border collies can work any type of stock, including sheep, cattle, poultry, and pigs. These dogs are the stock dog of choice for ranchers across the globe. The ideal working border collie has the perfect mixture of balance—the ability to find the exact right point in space and put the exact right amount of pressure on the sheep—and power. It is this combination that makes them the perfect dog to work livestock.
These dogs work using a method called "the stalk." This is a low, deliberate approach that moves sheep through presence rather than force. The stalk is what makes these dogs so unique, and it's a technique that's used when herding any type of stock, not just sheep.
Border collies are not a dog for everyone. But if you have the time and patience to learn what makes them tick, these dogs can be incredible, loyal companions. Just be sure to give them more than a daily walk. They need mental work, such as training, puzzles, structured games, or dog sports like agility or flyball, or ideally, actual herding.

Some people drive electric cars, use solar energy, shop with eco-friendly businesses. But what if you’re too busy to make a big environmental contribution? That doesn’t mean there’s nothing you can do to help. Even the simplest actions can make a difference. And if your environmental contributions can also be simple and practical, all the better. If you need ideas to get you started, here are a few:
Use rechargeable batteries
Rechargeable batteries cost a little more upfront, but they save you money over time. They also reduce the amount of hazardous waste that ends up in landfills. It’s a simple switch: buy packs in the most commonly used battery sizes and swap them in when current batteries run low.
Clean with reusable tools
Single-use cleaning products and tools like Swiffer mop and duster sheets and Clorox wipes are convenient, but when you consider large numbers of these single-use cleaning sheets piling up in landfills, they’re not good for the environment. Reusable mops and refillable eco-friendly cleaning products are equally convenient alternatives. You’ll also reduce the amount of toxic chemicals like ethyl alcohol, Alkyl Polyglucoside, and Didecyl Dimethyl Ammonium Chloride that end up in landfills.
Buy local
Food is currently shipped from all over the world. When you buy from local growers and farmers, it requires less energy for the transportation of food. Local farmers markets are one way to buy local food. And many grocery stores carry local foods. Often, they post signs near them saying they are local. This means you’re also consuming healthier food.
Avoid washing your car
Car washes generally use much less water than you would if you were to wash your car yourself. They also use high-powered machines to clean cars quickly and efficiently. And some car washes will also vacuum the inside of your car.
Try a dry-erase board
A dry-erase board stays in view so you’re less likely to misplace notes. It’s a great way to replace notepads and post-it notes for to-do lists, grocery lists, and family notes. You’ll also reduce the amount of waste.
A few simple changes can have a big impact. There are lots of ways to make a difference, even if you don’t have time to make a big environmental contribution.

What is the Value of a Warehouse?
Warehouses add value through physical activities, but also by gathering and maintaining related information and informing supply chain partners as required. In order to add value, a warehouse should support four basic functions:

High blood pressure is a serious health issue, and is the leading cause of cardiovascular disease, which is the leading cause of death worldwide. It’s important to monitor your blood pressure in order to take steps to reduce it. Here’s what you need to know about how and when to measure blood pressure:
When to Measure
Most doctors recommend measuring your blood pressure when you first wake up in the morning. However, because moving around and the stress of the day will increase your blood pressure, it’s a good idea to take it at the end of the day as well to see what your blood pressure levels look like during the day.
It’s important to measure at the same time every day. This could be in the morning or in the evening. Either way, consistency is key.
How to Measure
Before you start testing, make sure you take a few minutes to sit still and relax. Avoid exercise, smoking or caffeinated beverages for the thirty minutes before testing. Use the restroom before you start, and sit with your back straight and supported.
Place your feet flat on the floor with your legs uncrossed, and make sure your arm is at heart level to eliminate the influence of gravity on your reading. Rest your testing arm on a flat, supportive surface with the upper arm at chest level, and slide the cuff onto your arm so that the bottom of the cuff is under your clothing and just above your elbow. Make sure the cuff size is two-thirds the length of your arm from elbow to shoulder. A cuff that is too large or too small will give you artificially low or high readings.
Follow the instructions that come with your monitor. Take two to three readings each time you test your blood pressure. If you’re using a quality machine, you should get an accurate reading.
If you have hypertension, you should check your blood pressure more often. Talk to your doctor about how frequently you should be measuring and see if you need to check twice a day until your blood pressure is under control. Once your blood pressure is under control, you can reduce the frequency of testing while continuing to monitor your heart health.
How Often to Measure
At the very least, your blood pressure should be checked once every year at a doctor visit. If you have high blood pressure, you should check more frequently. Our German and Te Reo programmes are designed to help our students stand with confidence on a local marae or order a meal in a Berlin café. That means that at different stages, the programmes have different focuses and goals. In Year 10 for example, the Te Reo focus is formal language and marae tikanga, while the German focus is travel and everyday situations. The main goals of both programmes are to prepare students for NCEA Level 1 by correspondence, to give them a foundation for travel to German speaking countries if they wish, and to ensure that we always have a close liaison with our local marae.
German (Years 7-8)
Our German programme runs from Year 7 through to Year 10. In Year 7 and 8, we begin with an introduction to basic vocabulary and key phrases, learning to count to 100 and say the German alphabet. We also cover the basic geography of Germany, Austria and Switzerland. Year 7 and 8 students have a Te Reo lesson once a week for two terms, and learn to introduce themselves, talk about their family, age, birthday, where they are from and their house. In the second year they build on their language knowledge from the previous year, learning to talk about school subjects, pets, hobbies, sport, food and how to tell the time.
German (Years 9-10)
In Year 9 our programme builds on the basics covered in the junior school. In the odd year, our focus is on Te Marae (the marae), and our students learn to count to 100 and say the German alphabet. In the second year, we build on the language knowledge from the previous year, and our students learn to talk about school subjects, pets, hobbies, sport, food and how to tell the time. Year 9 students have two periods of Te Reo for two terms, and in the third Term, they have 3 German lessons a week. We extend our students’ vocabulary, using the computer programme ‘Languagenut’ to help them learn vocabulary. Our Year 10 German programme helps to create a foundation for students wishing to study German in Year 10. Our students continue to learn about the similarities and differences between German and New Zealand culture, and we teach them about accommodation and directions, travel and transport.
Te Reo Māori (Year 10)
Te Reo Māori is an option in Year 10. Our Year 10 Te Reo Māori programme is designed to prepare students with confidence and skill to study NCEA Level 1 by correspondence. Our focus in Year 10 is on formal language, marae tikanga, including pōwhiri (welcome ceremonies), roles on the marae and appropriate behaviour. We also study tikanga of the marae, including describing people, places and events in more detail. Students leave with lasting skills: confidence in speaking, respect for other cultures, and a stronger connection to their own community.
